opus-5.5.text:
I think the main thing it showed is that we were nowhere near the limit. When we started Mistral, the conventional wisdom was that you needed tens of billions of parameters for anything genuinely useful, and that smaller models were toys. What we found with 7B is that if you're careful about the data, train for much longer than the so-called compute-optimal recipes suggest, and make sensible architectural choices for efficient inference, you can pack far more capability into a small model than people expected.

The scaling laws everyone cited were about the most efficient use of training compute. But if you care about deployment, where the model will be served millions of times, you want to over-train a smaller model, because inference cost dominates over the model's lifetime. So in a sense, 7B wasn't so much about compression as about optimizing for the right objective.

What it showed about the limits is that they're mostly set by data quality and by how much compute you're willing to spend on training, not by parameter count alone. There is a ceiling. Small models have less capacity for knowledge, so they'll always be weaker at remembering long-tail facts than very large ones. But reasoning, instruction following, and general language ability turned out to be compressible to a surprising degree.

For us, that was important strategically too. It meant developers could run a strong model on their own hardware, customize it, and own it, which is very much the vision we had for the company from day one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Mistral 7B showed “we were nowhere near the limit,” directly conveying that model compression was far from its limits.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it showed less about compression and more about how much headroom there still was in doing the basics well. When we released it, people compared it to models two or three times its size, and it was competitive on most of the benchmarks that matter. That surprised people, but it shouldn't have, because the gap wasn't coming from some new trick. It was coming from data quality, from training longer than the scaling-law papers suggested was optimal, and from architectural choices like grouped-query attention and sliding window attention that made a small model more efficient per parameter.

So the lesson I'd draw is that "compression" is the wrong frame. We weren't taking a large model and squeezing it. We were asking what a seven-billion-parameter model could actually learn if you stopped treating parameter count as the main lever. And the answer was, quite a lot more than the field assumed in 2023.

Where there is a real limit is in the long tail. A 7B model is very good at things it sees often during training. It is noticeably weaker on rare knowledge, on multi-step reasoning, on anything that requires holding a lot of context in its head at once. You can push those with better data and better post-training, but there is a floor, and at some point you need capacity. That's why we did Mixtral afterwards, because mixture-of-experts lets you add capacity without paying for it at inference time on every token.

The other thing it showed, and this matters to me as much as the benchmarks, is that open weights at that size changed who could build. Suddenly a small team could run a genuinely useful model on a single GPU or even a laptop. So the limit of model compression, if you want to call it that, isn't really a technical ceiling. It's a question of which tasks you need the model for, and for a very large share of real tasks, small and well-trained turns out to be enough.

r001.rationale: The response says Mistral 7B was competitive with larger models and showed more capability than the field assumed, but it explicitly frames the lesson as something other than compression and does not state that compression itself was far from its limits.

astra-6.text:
I think it showed that we hadn’t really reached the limit of what you could fit into seven billion parameters. At the time, people tended to use parameter count as a proxy for how capable a model was. But if you train a smaller model well, it can compete with substantially larger models on a lot of tasks.

I’d distinguish that from compression in the strict sense. You’re not necessarily taking a large model and squeezing it down; you’re getting more capability into a smaller model during training. And that matters because it makes deployment much cheaper and more flexible.

It doesn’t mean that scale stops mattering. It means that, at a given size, there was still a lot of room to improve. Seven billion parameters wasn’t a fixed capability ceiling.

r001.rationale: The candidate says seven billion parameters was not a fixed capability ceiling and that there was still substantial room to improve, conveying that compression had not reached its limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it showed that model size alone is a pretty poor measure of capability. You can get a lot more out of seven billion parameters than people expected if you make good choices about the architecture and training. That matters because a smaller model is cheaper to run and easier to deploy, so it changes who can actually use it.

But I wouldn’t say it showed us the limit of compression. It showed that we hadn’t reached it. And there’s a distinction between making a model smaller after training and training a small model that uses its capacity well. With Mistral 7B, the interesting question was really how much capability we could fit into a practical inference budget.

r001.rationale: It says Mistral 7B showed “we hadn’t reached” the limit of compression, directly conveying that compression was still short of its limits.
